'''''Ulex europaeus''''', commonly known as '''gorse''', '''common gorse''', '''furze''' or  '''whin''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] native to Western Europe.<ref name = POWO>{{cite web | url = https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:524298-1 | title = ''Ulex europaeus'' L. | publisher = Kew Science: Plants of the World Online | access-date = 2 January 2019}}</ref>

==Description==

Growing to {{Convert|4.5|m|sigfig=1}} tall, it is an evergreen [[shrub]].<ref name="Francis-Baker-2021">{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |page=46}}</ref> The young stems are green, with the [[Shoot (botany)|shoot]]s and [[leaves]] modified into green spines, {{Convert|1|-|3|cm|frac=4}} long.<ref name="Brickell-2008"/> Young seedlings produce normal leaves for the first few months; these are trifoliate, resembling a small [[clover]] leaf.

The solitary [[flower]]s are yellow, {{Convert|1–2|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, with the [[pea]]-flower structure typical of the Fabaceae; they are produced throughout the year, but mainly over a long period in spring. They are coconut-scented.<ref name="Brickell-2008">{{cite book | editor-last = Brickell | editor-first = Christopher | title = The Royal Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants | year = 2008 | page = 1062 | publisher = Dorling Kindersley | location = United Kingdom | ISBN = 978-1-4053-3296-5}}</ref> The [[fruit]] is a [[legume]] (pod) {{Convert|2|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, dark purplish-brown, partly enclosed by the pale brown remnants of the flower; the pod contains 2–3 small blackish, shiny, hard [[seed]]s, which are ejected when the pod splits open in hot weather. Seeds remain viable for 30 years.

Like many species of [[gorse]], it readily catches fire due to high levels of natural oils found in the spines.<ref name=":1" />  However, the plant can resprout from anywhere on the stem above the roots and the seeds remain viable after fire, so gorse can grow in recently burned areas.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zouhar |first=Kris |date=2005 |title=Ulex europaeus |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/shrub/uleeur/all.html#60 |journal=Fire Effects Information System |publisher=U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory |access-date=September 10, 2026}}</ref> 

It has a tap root, lateral and adventitious roots. An extremely tough and [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] plant, it survives temperatures down to {{convert|-20|C|F|abbr=on}}.<ref name="RHS">{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/18575/i-Ulex-europaeus-i/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Ulex europaeus''
| access-date = 1 January 2019}}</ref>  It can live for about thirty years.

==Ecology==
Like other legumes, it [[Nitrogen fixation|fixes nitrogen]] into the soil.<ref name="Gunasekera-2009" />

=== As an invasive species ===
The species has been introduced to other areas of Europe, and also to the [[Americas]], [[New Zealand]], [[South Africa]], and [[Australia]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Weeds of National Significance (WONS)|url=http://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/invasive/weeds/weeds/lists/wons.html|website=www.environment.gov.au|publisher=Commonwealth of Australia – Department of the Environment and Energy|access-date=30 November 2016|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.invasives.org.za/invasive-species/item/310-european-gorse%7Culex-europaeus.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140819084653/http://www.invasives.org.za/invasive-species/item/310-european-gorse%7Culex-europaeus.html | archive-date=2014-08-19 | title=European gorse | Ulex europaeus – Invasives Species South Africa| date=2014-08-19}}</ref> where it is often considered a [[weed]] and is a serious problem [[invasive species]] in some areas (notably the western United States, [[Chile]] and New Zealand). It was introduced to New Zealand from Britain as a type of [[Hedge (barrier)|hedge]], but became a major blight to farmers as the climate suited its growth better than its native habitat and many of its natural predators were absent.

Common gorse is also an invasive species in the montane grasslands of [[Horton Plains National Park]] in Sri Lanka. It outcompetes native, endemic species and is a fire hazard.<ref name="Gunasekera-2009">Lalith Gunasekera, ''Invasive Plants: A guide to the identification of the most invasive plants of Sri Lanka'', Colombo 2009, p. 88–89.</ref>

[[Biological pest control]] is used on this plant in many areas. The [[Tetranychus lintearius|gorse spider mite]] (''Tetranychus lintearius'') and the [[Exapion ulicis|gorse seed weevil]] (''Exapion ulicis'') reduce the spread of the plant, although their efficacy has varied.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |year=2015 |title=Gorse (Ulex europaeus) |journal=Oregon state noxious weed list}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
This plant is used for hedging, boundary definition and [[groundcover]] in suitably sunny, open locations. [[Cultivars]] include 'Strictus' (Irish gorse), a dwarf form, and the double-flowered, non-fruiting 'Flore Pleno', which has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector – ''Ulex europaeus'' 'Flore Pleno'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/85508/Ulex-europaeus-Flore-Pleno-(d)/Details | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 103 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 1 January 2019}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Whinstonedalgarven.JPG|thumb|Whin-stone, used for bruising gorse]]

Bruised gorse was used in some areas for feeding to horses and other livestock.<ref>Aiton, William (1811). ''General View of The Agriculture of the County of Ayr; observations on the means of its improvement; drawn up for the consideration of the Board of Agriculture, and Internal Improvements, with Beautiful Engravings''. Glasgow. p. 441</ref> The fragrant petals have a number of culinary uses.<ref name="Francis-Baker-2021" />

A [[lectin]] extracted from seeds of this species binds to, is remarkably specific for, and is the standard method for identification of [[H substance]] (absent in the [[hh antigen system]]) on human [[red blood cell]]s. The vast majority of humans express H substance, which is the basis for the [[ABO blood group system]], but a few rare individuals ("[[Bombay phenotype]]") do not—and a chemical isolated from ''U. europaeus'' is used to identify these individuals. This lectin is also used as a marker for human vascular [[endothelial cells]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Holthöfer|first=H.|last2=Virtanen|first2=I.|last3=Kariniemi|first3=A. L.|last4=Hormia|first4=M.|last5=Linder|first5=E.|last6=Miettinen|first6=A.|date=July 1982|title=Ulex europaeus I lectin as a marker for vascular endothelium in human tissues|journal=Laboratory Investigation; A Journal of Technical Methods and Pathology|volume=47|issue=1|pages=60–66|issn=0023-6837|pmid=6177923}}</ref> and as a tool for their isolation for ''in vitro'' culture.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Catravas|first=John D.|last2=Snead|first2=Connie|last3=Dimitropoulou|first3=Christiana|last4=Chang|first4=Albert S.Y.|last5=Lucas|first5=Rudolf|last6=Verin|first6=Alexander D.|last7=Black|first7=Stephen M.|title=Harvesting, identification and barrier function of human lung microvascular endothelial cells|journal=Vascular Pharmacology|volume=52|issue=5–6|pages=175–181|doi=10.1016/j.vph.2009.12.009|pmid=20060932|pmc=4374552|year=2010}}</ref>
